title: Vendor a library with subtree instead of submodules
summary: Subtree puts the library's files and history directly into your repository, so a plain clone just works. Add one, pull an upstream update, and push a fix back.
mental_model: A submodule stores a pointer; a subtree stores the files. With subtree, `git clone` gives you everything and nobody has to know the library is vendored — at the cost of the library's commits living in your history.

steps.title: Add the library as a subtree
steps.why: `subtree add --prefix` fetches the other repository and grafts its tree under that directory. `--squash` collapses its history into one commit, which keeps your log readable — without it you inherit every commit the library ever had.
steps.expect: The library's files under vendor/sensors, and two new commits describing the graft.

verify.label: the library's files are tracked in this repository

steps.title: See the difference from a submodule
steps.why: There is no `.gitmodules`, no gitlink, no special index entry — just ordinary files in an ordinary tree. That is the whole selling point: consumers need no extra commands.
commands: sh -c 'ls -a | grep gitmodules || echo "no .gitmodules — nothing to initialise"'
steps.expect: Mode 040000 for a normal tree, and 100644 files inside it.

steps.title: Prove a plain clone just works
steps.why: This is the payoff. A colleague clones and has the library immediately — no `--recurse-submodules`, no empty directory, no support question.
steps.expect: The library present in a fresh clone with no extra steps.

verify.label: a plain clone contains the vendored library
verify.hint: this is the submodule problem that subtree does not have

steps.title: Upstream releases a change
steps.why: The library moves on independently. Your repository knows nothing about it yet — subtree is a copy, so updates are a deliberate act, exactly like a dependency bump.
steps.expect: The upstream has three commits; your copy still has the old file.

steps.title: Pull the update in
steps.why: `subtree pull` fetches and merges the library's new commits under the prefix. With `--squash` it lands as a single readable commit rather than replaying the library's own history into yours.

actions.run: sh -c 'git subtree pull --prefix=vendor/sensors sensors main --squash -m "Update vendored sensors library"'

steps.expect: read_temp appears, in a commit that says what it is.

verify.label: the upstream update was pulled in

steps.title: Fix a bug in the vendored copy
steps.why: You can edit vendored files directly — they are just files. Commit it in your repository as normal; nothing special happens until you decide to send it upstream.

verify.label: the fix is an ordinary commit in your repository

steps.title: Send it back upstream
steps.why: `subtree push` extracts the commits that touched the prefix, rewrites their paths to the library's root, and pushes them to the other repository. This is the part submodules make easy and subtree makes possible-but-fiddly.
steps.expect: A branch in the library containing your change, with the vendor/ prefix stripped.

verify.label: the downstream fix reached the library, path-rewritten

steps.title: Weigh it against submodules
steps.why: Subtree: clones just work, no extra commands, but your history carries the library and updates are manual. Submodule: exact pinning and no history bloat, but every clone needs an extra step and detached HEADs bite people. Neither is wrong — pick per repository.
steps.expect: Nothing to run; this step is the trade-off summary.

verify.label: the library is vendored as ordinary tracked files
the upstream update and your own fix are both present
no submodule machinery — a plain clone is enough
a fresh clone got the library with no extra commands
the downstream fix was contributed back upstream

pitfalls: Without `--squash` the library's entire history is replayed into yours, and `git log` becomes unreadable. Use it unless you specifically want the detail.
`git subtree pull` must be run from the repository root, and the prefix must match exactly what you used for `add`. A typo silently creates a second copy.
`subtree push` walks every commit touching the prefix and can be very slow on a large history. `git subtree split --rejoin` speeds up later pushes.
Editing vendored files locally means diverging from upstream. Contribute the fix back, or record why you cannot — a forked vendored copy nobody remembers is a maintenance trap.
`git subtree` ships with git but is a contrib script; on some distributions it needs a separate package.
cheatsheet: extract the prefix's history as a branch
